Neil Simon. A playwright and screenwriter who lived from nineteen twenty-seven to twenty eighteen, his comedies are among the most-performed and commercially successful in American theatre. His work mines domestic relationships, family dysfunction, and urban Jewish life for both laughter and pathos. He was a master of comic timing and the emotional turn—making laughter the vehicle for genuine feeling.

The Odd Couple came in nineteen sixty-five, a comedy of two divorced men sharing an apartment that became a television and film classic. It exemplifies his ear for dialogue and character. Barefoot in the Park arrived in nineteen sixty-three as his debut play about newlyweds navigating marriage in a cramped New York apartment—an immediate success that established his style. The Sunshine Boys, appearing in nineteen seventy-two, gave us retired vaudeville comedians, demonstrating his ability to blend humor with melancholy and nostalgia for a lost world.

Simon won multiple Tony Awards, and his plays have been translated into numerous languages and remain staples of community and university theatres everywhere. He was equally accomplished as a screenwriter, adapting his own plays and writing original film scripts like The Goodbye Girl and The Poseidon Adventure. His comedy is grounded in specificity—Jewish New York, the rhythms of married life, the pathos underlying suburban conformity.

He represents one of American comedy's most successful and prolific voices. His plays define postwar Broadway comedy itself. While Arthur Miller engaged American social drama through tragedy, Simon's approach was primarily comedic. He captured the vulnerability of domestic life, how marriage and family reveal us to ourselves.
